blocks.text: Secure messaging has become central to modern enterprise operations, carrying sensitive correspondence, credentials, and operational data across distributed and increasingly mobile workforces. As organizations route a growing share of internal communication through chat platforms, these systems become high-value targets for data leakage, unauthorized access, impersonation, and insider misuse. Systematic threat-modeling studies of enterprise messaging confirm that many platforms lack rigorous security analysis and remain exposed to spoofing, tampering, information disclosure, and elevation-of-privilege attacks, with high-priority risks frequently traced to human factors and insider misuse as well as to integration points such as application programming interfaces and third-party services [P4]. The corresponding mitigation set proposed in that work, spanning end-to-end encryption, strong authentication, hardened endpoints, and anomaly-based monitoring, frames the design space within which a privacy-preserving messaging platform must operate [P4].

This review unifies three intertwined problem areas that current secure-messaging research treats largely in isolation. The first concerns authentication and the limits of contemporary end-to-end encryption (E2EE). A broad systematization of nineteen popular E2EE applications found that all of them implement only opportunistic E2EE, which defeats a passive man-in-the-middle adversary but remains vulnerable to an active attacker mounting key-substitution attacks through a malicious or coerced key-distribution server [P1]. The authentication ceremony that would upgrade an application to authenticated E2EE is optional in every application studied and depends on users locating, understanding, and correctly completing manual fingerprint comparisons, a process shown to fail routinely due to human error [P1]. Concrete E2EE implementations reinforce this gap: a Diffie-Hellman and AES-256 chat system built on a scalable microservice backend demonstrates strong confidentiality, yet its key exchange lacks an authentication mechanism and its phone-number-plus-SMS login is neither MitM-resistant nor privacy-preserving [P5].

The second problem area is the insider threat: malicious activity by users who already hold legitimate access credentials. Because such activity blends in with authorized behavior, it evades classical rule- and signature-based defenses, and the resulting damage far exceeds that of external attacks [P3]. Deep-learning sequence models, particularly long short-term memory (LSTM) and bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM) architectures, have emerged as the dominant approach for capturing the temporal and semantic patterns that distinguish malicious from benign user activity [P2], [P3]. A BiLSTM enhanced with grouped orthogonal initialization and Swish activation has been proposed for insider detection coupled with privacy-preserving data transfer [P2], and comprehensive surveys validate this model family on benchmark datasets while explicitly championing privacy-preserving detection through federated learning, differential privacy, and on-endpoint analysis [P3]. Threat-modeling work likewise identifies insider misuse as a high-priority enterprise risk and calls for fusing AI-driven anomaly detection with systematic security analysis [P4].

The third problem area is the need for privacy-preserving, on-device threat detection. Sending message content to cloud services for analysis introduces latency and exposes sensitive data, motivating detection that runs locally on the user's device. Surveys of anomaly detection map a rich landscape of machine- and deep-learning techniques, including LSTM and autoencoder approaches demonstrated on Android, while highlighting challenges of noisy data, scarce labels, limited memory, and real-time streaming that constrain edge deployment [P9]. Lightweight transformer models address these constraints directly: an Aquila-optimized TinyBERT detector for smishing (SMS phishing) on Android reached 96.81% accuracy with deliberately short training to remain device-suitable [P10], while the PHILDER framework selected an undersampled TinyBERT for the best balance of accuracy and computational cost, reporting 99.27% phishing-detection accuracy under composite efficiency metrics [P11]. URL-only hybrid classifiers further show that compact models can reach 98.12% accuracy with low latency and no third-party dependency [P12]. Together these results establish the feasibility of accurate, low-resource threat classification suitable for frameworks such as TensorFlow Lite.

Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) offer a principled answer to the authentication and privacy gap that manual ceremonies fail to close. A ZKP allows a prover to convince a verifier that a statement is true without revealing any information beyond its validity, enabling authentication that never transmits passwords or secrets [P6]. Non-interactive constructions such as zk-SNARKs, realized in part through the Fiat-Shamir heuristic, provide succinct and fast-to-verify proofs that remove the heavy multi-round exchange of interactive protocols, while delivering native anonymity and man-in-the-middle resistance at lower overhead than public-key infrastructure [P6], [P7]. A blockchain identity-management system built on the Pinocchio/Groth16 zk-SNARK family demonstrates password-less, secret-less anonymous authentication on a real deployment stack, but its 192 MB proving key and approximately 37-second proof generation also serve as a clear warning of the resource costs that a mobile-first design must engineer around [P8]. Replacing fragile fingerprint-verification ceremonies with non-interactive zk-SNARK authentication therefore directly targets the human-error gap identified in the secure-messaging literature [P1], [P6], [P7], [P8].

These observations motivate SentriZK, a conceptual design for a privacy-preserving, mobile-first Android secure-messaging platform that unifies three pillars: zero-knowledge-proof authentication using non-interactive Groth16 zk-SNARKs to authenticate users without transmitting passwords or secrets; on-device, lightweight AI threat detection adapting deep-learning insider-threat, anomaly, and phishing/smishing models to run locally via TensorFlow Lite; and end-to-end encrypted transport built on Diffie-Hellman key exchange and AES-256. SentriZK is presented at the design and review stage, and this paper is a literature review that motivates and proposes its conceptual architecture rather than reporting experimental results. The contributions of this review are fourfold: it synthesizes the evidence base across the three problem domains of authentication and E2EE, insider-threat detection, and on-device threat detection; it shows how non-interactive zero-knowledge authentication addresses the documented authentication and privacy gaps of current E2EE messengers; it identifies the open challenges and resource constraints that bound a mobile deployment; and it derives from this synthesis the unified architecture proposed for SentriZK.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. The Methodology section describes the source-selection and analysis procedure underlying the review. Three domain review sections then examine, in turn, secure messaging with authentication and end-to-end encryption [P1], [P4], [P5]; insider-threat detection using machine and deep learning [P2], [P3]; and privacy-preserving, on-device anomaly and phishing/smishing detection [P9], [P10], [P11], [P12], alongside zero-knowledge authentication [P6], [P7], [P8]. A synthesis and gaps section consolidates the cross-domain findings and the open challenges they expose. The proposed architecture section then presents the unified SentriZK design, after which the conclusion summarizes the review and outlines future work.
